implementation_notes: The splitter is an adapter chain: flat_map maps one composite into its parts and flattens them into the iterator, slice::chunks(n) yields fixed-size parts, and the send loop is a plain for over the result, so nothing beyond the current part is materialised. Ownership is the design pressure: parts borrow from the composite, so anything that outlives the loop (an async publish, a spawned task) must own its bytes. The classic role structure only reappears with an async runtime, where the framed variant takes over.
pitfalls: flat_map yields items borrowed from the composite: a part that must outlive the loop needs owned bytes (Bytes/String), otherwise the borrow checker forces 'static bounds through the whole signature.
Iterator adapters are lazy, so a chain that is never driven by a for/collect publishes nothing at all.
Iterators are single-use: a stored iterator cannot be restarted after it is exhausted, and collecting it to reuse it recreates the memory problem the split was meant to avoid.

variants.name: Stream framing with tokio_util codecs (FramedRead + Decoder)
variants.implementation_notes: When the composite is a byte stream rather than a decoded document, the splitter is the runtime's framing layer: implement Decoder - decode(&mut BytesMut) returns Option<Self::Item> - and FramedRead turns the socket or file into a stream of frames, each frame becoming one message, while state kept on the decoder carries the partial frame across reads. That is precisely the boundary-detection responsibility the classic Splitter owns, and decode_eof exists because files and FIFOs can read zero bytes at EOF (the decoder decides whether a frame may cross that boundary). Use it for length-prefixed or delimiter-framed protocols; use the iterator form when the payload is already parsed.
pitfalls: Returning Ok(Some(..)) without consuming the bytes from src makes Framed spin forever on the same buffer; split_to/advance is mandatory.
The default decode_eof returns Ok(None), so a stream can end with a partial frame still in src - handle trailing data explicitly when the protocol allows it.
A decoder that allocates a fresh buffer per frame without a maximum frame length lets a peer exhaust memory (cap the frame size).
